newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu survives no-confidence motion.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu survives no-confidence motion.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu survived a no-confidence vote in parliament on Monday and his foreign minister insisted agreement with the PLO on a long-delayed redeployment in Hebron may be only days away.
Their right-wing coalition handily defeated the no-confidence motion -- the second of its four-month-old term -- by a vote of 55-49 with two abstentions. The result had been expected.

Israeli opposition parties, including those that launched peace moves with the PLO when in power, submitted the motion. Netanyahu ousted Labour party prime minister Shimon Peres on a campaign against the Hebron deal and other peace moves.
Foreign Minister David Levy insisted that barring a last-minute retreat in positions, a deal was close with the PLO on the long-promised Israeli troop pullback from the West Bank city of Hebron.
"It's not a matter of weeks but perhaps a number of days...but there are additional issues facing us," Levy told parliament.
Earlier Netanyahu said he would meet Palestinian President Yasser Arafat when a Hebron deal was near.
"So far, we have not set a time for such a meeting so you can assess where we are on the basis of that," he told reporters.
Western diplomats said the two sides were trying to close a deal on Hebron before U.S. elections on November 5.

But PLO officials said U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross had yet to bridge wide gaps. Hebron is the last and most sensitive of seven West Bank cities due to be given self-rule in an Israeli-PLO peace deal signed last year.
The two sides are due to resume formal U.S.-mediated negotiations at Egypt's Red Sea resort of Taba on Tuesday.
The redeployment should have been carried out in March but was delayed by Peres's government following Islamic militant suicide bombings that killed 59 people in Israel.

The pullback was frozen by Netanyahu, who has demanded changes in the deal he said were necessary to ensure the security of some 400 Israeli settlers who live amidst 100,000 Palestinians in the city holy to Jews and Moslems.
Palestinians reject any renegotiation of the signed accord.
